transcript:
Header:
Date: 2025-08-05
Start: 09:43 PDT
Duration: 49 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Liam Ortiz (Redwood SE), Priya Nair (Sable Head of ML), Tom Ellis (Sable Platform Eng), Rafael Gomez (CTO)
---
Summary (auto): demo of Redwood Optimize recommendations for batching and caching; discussed cost model assumptions and next steps for benchmarks.
---
00:00 Maya Chen: good morning everyone thanks for making time today uh i'm maya from redwood inference, i'm the account lead for sable systems. Liam's gonna take most of the technical walkthrough.
00:08 Liam Ortiz: hey all, quick agenda — show optimize console, talk batching presets, demo session/prefix cache impact, run through cost model calc, then q&a and bench plan. sound ok?
00:18 Priya Nair: yep looks good. we mostly care about steady high-concurrency chat — 200-300 concurrent users during peak, average seq len around 180 tokens, tails to 1k.
00:30 Tom Ellis: also to flag we have strict residency requirements — EU region first, and we'll want SSO and KMS for production.
00:40 Liam Ortiz: noted. i'll show region-aware routing and where KMS config is surfaced in the private deployment doc later.
00:48 Maya Chen: quick qualification — are you currently on a managed endpoint or self-hosted?
00:52 Priya Nair: hybrid — some experiments on open-source endpoints, but cost/ops overhead is high. evaluating dedicated or hosted depending on SLA.
01:05 Liam Ortiz: perfect. okay jumping into the Optimize tab — apologies if auto-caption's a little off, the console screenshot i shared should help (link: /deck/optimize-console-sable.png). first slide is recommended batching policy: target batch size 16 for your seq distribution, concurrency cap at 48 per shard.
01:25 Rafael Gomez: how do you get to 16? our current requests are mostly 1-2 prompts per session with heavy context preface.
01:33 Liam Ortiz: good question. the 16 comes from simulated packing given your median seq len — smaller seqs pack well into a batch until you hit memory limits. the cost model uses tokens per second and kernel saturation to estimate throughput. if your median is 180, 16 is a sweet spot for A100-like GPUs.
01:55 Tom Ellis: what about prefix vs session cache — what's best for our use case?
02:02 Liam Ortiz: short answer: prefix cache (we sometimes call it prefetch/prefetch but console labels it prefix) is best when large parts of the prompt are identical across requests — like system message + knowledge bits. session/KV cache is better for long multi-turn state where you keep the kv cache across requests for the same session id. for chat with personalized context, a hybrid approach often wins.
02:28 Priya Nair: our app has 60% identical system context, and 40% per-user history. so hybrid sounds plausible. how does that affect cost?
02:36 Liam Ortiz: on the cost model slide — if you enable prefix cache for the 60% repeated tokens, you get effective token savings close to that fraction minus miss-rate. then session cache reduces repeated decoding work for multi-turn. in practice we've seen 25-45% cost reduction compared to no caching for similar mixes.
02:58 Maya Chen: i'll flag that the console's expected savings are a simulation — they'll change once we run real traffic benchmarks. that's where liam's proposed benchmark comes in.
03:08 Tom Ellis: there's a note in the doc about cold starts and KV cache warmup — can you explain that?
03:12 Liam Ortiz: yeah. cold starts happen if your session hasn't been used on that shard — the KV cache needs filling as you decode tokens. prefix cache avoids that because identical prefixes are pre-materialized and stored in memory; session cache requires token generation at least once per session to populate, so you see a latency spike on first couple of requests. the Optimize console shows estimated warmup cost and suggests prefetch windows.
03:37 Priya Nair: you mentioned prefetch window — what's the recommended lookahead?
03:40 Liam Ortiz: for your workload i'd recommend a prefetch window of 2-3 requests or 512-1024 tokens depending on how dynamic the user context is. too large and you waste memory, too small and you don't amortize the cost.
03:55 Rafael Gomez: how do we measure the real savings? do you provide a spreadsheet?
03:58 Maya Chen: yes — we'll send a tailored cost model that includes your token histogram, price per token (hosted vs dedicated), batching efficiency curves, and prefix/session cache hit rate sensitives. i'll put that in next steps.
04:10 Liam Ortiz: demoing the spreadsheet now — i'm sharing a very small sample with three scenarios: baseline (no cache), prefix-only, hybrid (prefix+session). assumptions: model: redwood-7b-quant, hosted price $X per 1k tokens (note: auto-transcribed $X may be wrong), dedicated reserved unit price using commit. baseline cost per million tokens in this sim is about $Y; prefix-only reduces it by ~28%; hybrid by ~36% assuming 70% prefix hit and 60% session hit after warmup.
04:48 Tom Ellis: those percentages are optimistic. what's sensitivity to hit rate?
04:51 Liam Ortiz: there's a sensitivity tab — if prefix hit drops to 40% your saving drops to single digits; caching benefits are highly hit-rate dependent. that's why we push for sample data from Priya.
05:05 Priya Nair: ok i'll send the CSV. what about latency? we can't exceed 250ms P95 for interactive flows.
05:12 Liam Ortiz: batching helps throughput but increases tail latency for single-request flows unless you use dynamic batching policies (we call them latency-bound vs throughput-bound presets). for P95 under 250ms, we'd run smaller max batch sizes and prefer session cache to avoid repeated decoding. Optimize offers profiles you can simulate against your token distribution.
05:40 Maya Chen: quick interruption — security question from Rafael?
05:43 Rafael Gomez: yeah, SOC2 + KMS — can we enable customer-managed keys in hosted or do we need private?
05:49 Liam Ortiz: customer-managed KMS is supported in Private deployments; hosted supports envelope encryption with Redwood-managed keys today but we've got Bring-Your-Own-Key options on roadmap and some partners already on custom HSM. for enterprise we'd recommend Private if KMS BYOK is a hard requirement.
06:10 Tom Ellis: any audit logs for token-level debugging?
06:13 Maya Chen: console has token-level cost traces and per-request traces, but the raw transcript of user text is redacted in logs unless you opt-in. we also surface audit logs for admin actions in dedicated/private.
06:26 Priya Nair: demo the actual Optimize UI settings you recommended?
06:30 Liam Ortiz: sure. switching to console — top-right presets: \"Throughput-Heavy\", \"Balanced\", \"Latency-Heavy\". for your peak we recommended Balanced with aggressive prefix caching. under caching tab toggle prefix cache, set TTL 24h for shared system prompts, prefetch window 2 requests, session cache keepalive 30m.
07:05 Priya Nair: TTL 24h — does that imply data retention concerns? is it encrypted at rest?
07:11 Liam Ortiz: yes encrypted at rest; retention policy can be configured — for EU residency we can pin region and retention to comply. the console shows where to set region and retention.
07:24 Rafael Gomez: you mentioned quantization earlier — any recommendations?
07:27 Liam Ortiz: 4-bit quantization can reduce GPU memory and increase effective batch capacity with minor quality impact for many workloads. our Optimize tab can recommend quant profiles based on your evals. it'll show expected tokens per second improvement and any quality delta we measure on your prompt set.
07:50 Maya Chen: switching back to economics — for the benchmark plan, liam suggested a 30- to 60-minute run with replayed traffic at X rps to capture packing behavior and warmup. can we agree on target rps?
07:59 Priya Nair: let's target 600 rps for peak sim and 150 rps for baseline.
08:05 Liam Ortiz: sounds good. we'll need a 2M request trace or representative sample — priya will provide. we'll produce a report with token-level breakdown, achieved batching stats, cache hit rates, and cost/savings projection.
08:20 Tom Ellis: one more thing — what happens when capacity is constrained? do you fall back to smaller model?
08:25 Liam Ortiz: yes policy routing can fallback to compatible model variants — that's configured per route with fallback rules. you can set cost vs latency thresholds for automatic fallback.
08:34 Priya Nair: could you put a note about consistent quality across fallback? we need to ensure no big regressions.
08:39 Liam Ortiz: absolutely — Optimize ties rollouts to evals so you can set quality gates and automatic rollback.
08:46 Rafael Gomez: any compliance docs to review for private deployment?
08:49 Maya Chen: i'll share the SOC2/ISO packet and the private deployment checklist.
08:54 Priya Nair: (murmur) thanks.
08:57 Liam Ortiz: quick callouts — watch out for these pitfalls: 1) overlarge batch sizes blowing memory, 2) wrong prefetch TTL causing stale context, 3) assuming perfect prefix hit rates. console has warnings for each.
09:12 Tom Ellis: how long to spin up dedicated capacity for pilot?
09:15 Maya Chen: for dedicated we can get a pilot pool in 2-3 weeks depending on procurement; hosted pilot can start in days. procurement will need the subscription and SOC docs.
09:26 Priya Nair: budget question — roughly how much difference hosted vs dedicated for our projected token volumes?
09:31 Liam Ortiz: depends on commit level — the sheet has an illustrative row: hosted baseline $A per month, dedicated with 12-month commit reduces unit cost by ~30% in the sim. exact numbers after we run benchmark.
09:44 Rafael Gomez: thanks. can you repeat the next steps?
09:47 Maya Chen: sure — i'll send the cost spreadsheet + security packet (Maya). Liam will run the benchmark when priya sends the trace. priya will send token histogram and trace. tom will confirm security contacts. schedule follow-up week of Aug 18.
09:58 Priya Nair: sounds good. thanks everyone.
10:02 Maya Chen: thanks all, we'll follow up in email.
